svg.title: Density altitude: a worked example with numbers
svg.desc: Worked example. Pressure altitude 5,000 feet. Standard temperature there is 15 minus 2 times 5, which is 5 degrees C. The outside air is 25 degrees C, 20 degrees above standard. A common rule of thumb is about 120 feet of density altitude per degree C, so about 2,400 feet, and the density altitude is about 7,400 feet. On a cold morning at minus 5 degrees C, 10 degrees below standard, the density altitude is about 1,200 feet lower, about 3,800 feet. The rule of thumb is approximate; use the chart or flight computer.
svg.text: Density altitude: a worked example with numbers
From pressure altitude and temperature to density altitude. Invented numbers; use your chart
or flight computer for the exact figure.
Hot day at a field with a pressure altitude of 5,000 ft
Density altitude: about 5,000 + 2,400 = 7,400 ft. The airplane performs as though it were up there.
Same field, cold morning: the other way
Outside air -5 C is 10 C below the standard 5 C: about 10 x 120 = 1,200 ft lower. Density
altitude is about 3,800 ft, below the 5,000 ft pressure altitude, so the airplane does better
Pressure altitude comes from the altimeter setting (previous diagram); standard temperature
The 120 ft per degree figure is a common rule of thumb, not an exact law: the chart or flight
Hot, high and humid days raise density altitude the most. Takeoff roll and climb get worse as
Source: PHAK (FAA-H-8083-25C) ch. 11, Performance. The 120 ft per C figure is a rule of thumb, not
